In late 2020, Elon wanted to eliminate the heavy landing legs planned for Starship’s booster. He asked:

“Why don’t we try to use the tower to catch it?”

Most engineers argued against the idea. If the booster crashed into the tower, it could stop future launches for a long time. After more than an hour of debate, the team was leaning toward keeping the legs.

Elon decided to pursue the catch.

Inspired by Mr. Miyagi catching a fly in The Karate Kid, he called the arms “chopsticks” and the tower “Mechazilla.”

His reasoning was simple:

“Legs would certainly work, but the best part is no part.”

Years of engineering turned that idea into real booster catches. Today, SpaceX caught the Starship upper stage for the first time.

What began as a question in a room at Starbase became history in front of the world.

Respect to Elon and every SpaceX employee who helped make it happen.

Source: Elon Musk by Walter Isaacson.

Yes, the green flame is caused by burning copper from depleting fuel in the regenerative cooling circuit and going oxygen-rich (closer to stoichiometric temperature) in the main combustion chamber. 

Slight underperformance of engines on this flight is the reason. The booster is meant to land with tiny residuals, so the solution is to improve engine performance and performance consistency (underway with Raptor V3.2), as well as adjust flight software to do MECO1 about one second earlier to ensure enough propellant for boostback and landing (tiny change).

These early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand, so this booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights.
